title: COP-31: Nepal takes climate disaster realities to global stage - Khabarhub
description: COP-31: Nepal takes climate disaster realities to global stage  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: From villages swept away by glacial floods to hydropower infrastructure reduced to rubble, Nepal’s mounting climate crisis is set to take centre stage at the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP-31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), beginning today in Antalya, Türkiye.

Carrying accounts of devastating floods, human casualties, destroyed settlements and billions of rupees in economic losses, Nepal is heading to the global climate summit with a clear message: countries that contribute least to global warming should not be left to bear its most devastating consequences.

The August 26 floods in the Bhote Koshi River, which caused widespread devastation in Rasuwa, remain among the most painful reminders of Nepal’s growing vulnerability to climate-induced disasters. The disaster left more than 1,450 people dead and over 5,000 missing, according to the figures cited in the disaster account, while inflicting enormous damage to public infrastructure, private property and livelihoods.

Before communities could recover from the tragedy, another devastating flood accompanied by mudslides struck the Budhigandaki River in Gorkha on September 25, adding to the country’s mounting disaster burden.

These were not isolated incidents. Last year, a glacial lake outburst triggered flooding in the Lende River, causing significant loss of life and property. Two years earlier, a sudden flood carrying massive amounts of mud and debris swept through Thame in Khumbu Pasanglhamu Rural Municipality of Solukhumbu, turning a thriving settlement into a scene of devastation.

The repeated destruction of settlements along the Bhote Koshi, Budhigandaki and Lende rivers, as well as Thame, illustrates the increasingly dangerous conditions facing Himalayan communities.

These disasters represent more than individual tragedies. They are manifestations of a wider climate crisis unfolding across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, where rising temperatures, accelerated snow and ice melt, and growing risks of glacial lake outburst floods are threatening communities, infrastructure and ecosystems.

For Nepal, which contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions but faces disproportionate climate risks, the issue is not simply one of disaster management. It is increasingly a question of climate justice, international responsibility and equitable access to climate finance.

Against this backdrop, Nepal is participating in COP-31 with the intention of bringing the realities of its vulnerable mountain communities before the international community and pressing for stronger global action on climate change.

Nepal delegation to highlight mountain vulnerability

A Nepali delegation comprising Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal and Minister for Health and Food Hygiene Nisha Mehta has already departed for Türkiye to participate in the conference. Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Geeta Chaudhary is scheduled to leave on Tuesday.

Minister Khanal will deliver Nepal’s statement during the inaugural high-level session, while Minister Chaudhary will lead the technical negotiations. Minister Mehta is expected to highlight the consequences of the climate crisis for public health and the country’s health sector.

The conference will bring together representatives of 192 parties to the UNFCCC, including heads of state, heads of government, ministers and senior officials, alongside climate scientists, development partners and civil society representatives.

Nepal’s delegation also includes Agriculture, Forest and Environment Ministry Secretary Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra and Climate Change Management Division Chief Dr Maheshwar Dhakal. They will participate in technical discussions, side events and programmes at the Nepal Pavilion to present the country’s priorities and advance its interests in international climate negotiations.

Dr Dharmaraj Upreti, Executive Chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, will draw attention to recent climate-related disasters, including the August 26 floods in Rasuwa’s Bhote Koshi River and the September 25 flooding in the Budhigandaki River.

Climate experts Manjit Dhakal, Raju Pandit Chhetri and Yugan Manandhar are also among those expected to advocate for Nepal’s climate priorities.

Political leaders, parliamentarians, government officials, civil society representatives and stakeholders from various governmental and non-governmental organisations are also expected to contribute to Nepal’s engagement at the conference.

Climate finance and the 1.5-degree target at the centre of Nepal’s agenda

Nepal has already made public its national position paper ahead of COP-31, outlining its priorities for the negotiations. The document continues to place mountain-related climate challenges, climate finance, loss and damage, and adaptation at the centre of the country’s international advocacy.

A key priority will be urging the international community to take more ambitious measures to limit the rise in global average temperatures to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

For Nepal, the 1.5-degree target has particular significance. Even a relatively small increase in global temperatures can intensify the risks facing Himalayan ecosystems, accelerate glacier loss and increase the threat of glacial lake outburst floods, with potentially devastating consequences for downstream communities.

Nepal is also expected to press for greater financial and technical support for climate-vulnerable mountain countries, particularly in addressing loss and damage, strengthening early warning systems, building resilient infrastructure and supporting communities facing climate-related displacement and livelihood disruptions.

Minister Chaudhary said Nepal would prioritise climate justice, mountain-related concerns, loss and damage, and climate finance during the conference.

“Nepal’s national priorities and the realities of the climate crisis will be presented forcefully to the international community,” she said.

She added that Nepal had prepared its national position paper for COP-31, giving particular attention to issues shared by mountain countries.

This year, Nepal and Bhutan have also jointly advanced the agenda of ‘1.5 degrees Celsius temperature increase and mountain areas’, seeking greater international recognition of the particular vulnerability of mountain ecosystems and communities.

For Nepal, COP-31 is therefore an opportunity to move beyond presenting disaster statistics and highlight the human, economic and environmental consequences of a warming planet.

The challenge will be to translate these realities into stronger international commitments, predictable climate financing and concrete measures to protect vulnerable mountain communities. As increasingly frequent disasters threaten lives, livelihoods and development gains, Nepal’s central demand is that the international response must match the scale and urgency of the crisis confronting the Himalayas.

Nepal to press for climate justice, predictable loss-and-damage financing

Highlighting the far-reaching consequences of global warming on mountains, glaciers, glacial lakes and the broader Himalayan ecosystem, Minister Chaudhary said the climate crisis was increasingly threatening multiple sectors, including agriculture, hydropower, food security, river systems and human livelihoods.

She stressed that adequate financial resources, technology transfer and institutional capacity development were essential to help mountain communities adapt to the rapidly changing climate.

Climate justice will also feature prominently in Nepal’s agenda, she said, noting that despite the country’s negligible contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions, it continues to suffer disproportionately from the consequences of climate change.

Chaudhary said Nepal would draw international attention to the humanitarian, economic and non-economic losses caused by devastating floods and landslides, particularly in the Bhote Koshi-Rasuwa region.

“Countries affected by climate change should receive equitable support. Nepal will insist that countries suffering loss and damage have access to adequate, predictable and easily accessible financial resources from the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage,” she said.

Nepal Pavilion to host more than 40 side events

For the first time, Nepal is preparing to establish its own national pavilion at COP-31, where it plans to organise more than 40 side events to showcase the country’s climate challenges, experiences and policy priorities.

According to the ministry, the Nepal Pavilion will serve as a common platform to bring the country’s climate realities and the experiences of local communities to the international stage. It will also provide space for the voices of young people, women, civil society, the private sector and other stakeholders to be heard in global climate discussions.

As part of efforts to strengthen international cooperation on mountain-related issues, Nepal is planning a high-level event on November 12 in collaboration with Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Bhutan and Pakistan.

The programme, titled ‘Advancing the Mountain Agenda: Glaciers, Cryosphere and Resilience under Overshoot, Shared Responsibility and Sustainable Financing’, will focus on the growing threats to mountain ecosystems and the need for collective international action and sustainable financing.

Another side event, titled ‘Strengthening Mountain Resilience through Adaptation Finance’, will be organised jointly by Nepal, Bhutan, Kyrgyzstan and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).

Chaudhary said the initiatives were expected to strengthen international discussions on glacier loss, the cryosphere, mountain resilience and access to adaptation finance.

Nepal and South Korea plan carbon trading agreement

On the bilateral cooperation front, Nepal is preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the government of South Korea on carbon trading.

Chaudhary said the proposed agreement would open new avenues for cooperation between the two countries in developing carbon markets and advancing climate change mitigation efforts.

She also emphasised that Nepal’s engagement at COP-31 would extend beyond government representation, with participation from civil society, local communities, youth, women, the private sector, experts and media representatives receiving particular attention.

Describing COP-31 as more than an international diplomatic gathering, Chaudhary said the conference offered Nepal an important opportunity to present the realities of the climate crisis, build common positions among mountain countries, reinforce its demand for climate justice and expand international cooperation and support.

She called for constructive engagement and support from all political parties, civil society organisations, the private sector, development partners, experts and media to ensure that Nepal’s national interests and climate priorities are effectively represented on the international stage.

Nepal to highlight adaptation, food security and climate finance

Dr Maheshwar Dhakal, Chief of the Climate Change Management Division at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, said Nepal would raise a broad range of issues, including climate adaptation, loss and damage, agriculture, food security, public health, climate finance and technology transfer.

He said the Nepali delegation would also emphasise rising temperatures in mountain regions, climate justice, international cooperation, emissions reduction, carbon markets, capacity development and a just transition.

Nepal’s position paper has also incorporated cross-cutting concerns, including gender equality and the disproportionate effects of climate change on children, young people, persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples and minority communities.

Meanwhile, Dr Dharmaraj Upreti, Executive Chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Nepal would present evidence of human casualties and physical destruction caused by climate-related disasters, including the devastating floods in the Bhote Koshi region of Rasuwa.

He said Nepal would use these examples to strengthen its international advocacy for adequate compensation, financial assistance and climate justice for countries and communities bearing the consequences of climate change despite having contributed little to the problem.

title: Nepal’s share market weathers political jitters - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s share market weathers political jitters  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Share investors were anxious on Thursday morning about how the market would perform amid speculation that a senior political leader could be arrested.

Investor and analyst Ajit Khanal took to Facebook to flag Thursday’s trading as particularly sensitive, saying the market could be more volatile than usual and needed close attention.

His concern stemmed from an issue that might appear unrelated to the stock market: rumours circulating since early morning that a top politician could be arrested.

The market reflected similar anxiety, falling by as much as 25 points during trading. However, it recovered some ground before the 4 pm close, limiting its loss to 12 points.

This is not the first time political developments and arrests have unsettled Nepal’s share market. Such reactions have occurred repeatedly since the Rastriya Swatantra Party assumed power.

Controversial businessman Deepak Bhatta was arrested on April 2. The market reopened on April 8 after a public holiday and the Nepal Stock Exchange (Nepse) index plunged 105 points in a single session.

About a month and a half later, on May 12, Jyoti Prakash Pandey, chief executive officer of Nepal Investment Mega Bank, was arrested. The market fell by 39 points that day.

The pattern has continued, with the market reacting to businesspeople being arrested and major political developments.

Investor and analyst Subash Chandra Dhungana said the market was sensitive to such incidents because investors preferred a stable environment.

“The stock market always seeks peace. But when businesspeople or political figures are arrested, or there is a possibility of their arrest, the market reacts in some way,” Dhungana said.

He said investors were also concerned because arrests had often taken place shortly before public holidays in the past, raising fears that a similar incident could occur again ahead of the Tihar holidays.

However, Tara Prasad Phulel, president of the Share Investors Association, said political developments were not the only factor affecting the market.

“Political developments have had an impact on the market. At the same time, investors are preparing for the festive season, and the market will remain closed for about a week. Nepse has yet to establish a clear trend,” he said.

The festive season was also reflected in Friday’s trading, when turnover fell to its lowest level since October 26. Shares worth Rs3.46 billion were traded.

Market remains above its average

The share market is currently trading above its average level.

The Nepse index is above the middle line of the Bollinger Bands, a technical indicator developed by John Bollinger in the 1980s. The indicator tracks market movements within an upper and lower band.

When the market approaches the upper band, it indicates relatively strong buying pressure. Near the lower band, it suggests stronger selling pressure.

The indicator also measures market volatility. The bands had widened when volatility was high in recent weeks, but their movement now suggests that fluctuations have eased somewhat.

When the upper and lower bands move closer together, volatility is generally lower. Wider bands indicate greater market fluctuations.

Buying and selling remain balanced

The Relative Strength Index (RSI) suggests that the market’s average gains are currently greater than its average losses.

The RSI measures market momentum by comparing the pace of price increases with that of declines. American technical analyst J Welles Wilder developed the calculation method in 1978.

The indicator generally uses changes in the market index over the previous 14 trading sessions. It calculates the average gains on days when the market rises and the average losses on days when it falls.

The RSI ranges from zero to 100.

A reading below 30 is generally considered to indicate strong selling pressure, while a reading above 70 suggests strong buying pressure. Between 30 and 70, buying and selling are generally considered more balanced.

The RSI stood at 55.82 on Friday. It had risen from 50 to as high as 58 before easing after Thursday’s market decline.

Buying outweighs selling

The accumulation and distribution (A/D) indicator also suggests that buying activity exceeded selling on Friday.

Accumulation indicates that investors are building positions, while distribution signals increased selling.

The distribution reading stood at 1 million on Friday, indicating that buying pressure was stronger that day. On Thursday, the indicator had shown a distribution reading of 1.8 million.

title: Nepal’s game developers seek tax relief, Google access to scale globally - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s game developers seek tax relief, Google access to scale globally  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah recently brought Nepal’s gaming industry into the spotlight when he invited representatives of game development companies and software developers to Singha Durbar to discuss the sector’s prospects and challenges.

During the meeting, Shah asked how games developed in Nepal were performing and showed interest in globally popular titles such as Clash of Clans. He also brought up GTA VI, the much-anticipated release from US gaming giant Rockstar Games, and asked about its potential impact.

The sixth major instalment in the best-selling Grand Theft Auto series, GTA VI is among the most anticipated video game releases worldwide. Its predecessor, GTA V, came out in 2013, and the new edition, arriving 13 years later, is reportedly the most expensive video game ever made, with development costs estimated at more than $1 billion.

The discussion has raised hopes among Nepali game developers that the government may finally address longstanding policy and regulatory obstacles holding back an industry with the potential to earn foreign currency and create high-value jobs.

Following the meeting, Shah wrote on Facebook on Saturday that his government would work to create conditions for Nepal to produce a global unicorn in the gaming and information technology sectors.

In technology and startup terminology, a unicorn is a privately held new venture valued at $1 billion or more, equivalent to over Rs151.3 billion.

Shah said the government had begun work to address tax and policy hurdles facing the gaming and IT industries. He also pledged investment in game jams, startup events, and hackathons (intensive collaborative coding competitions), alongside regular dialogue between industry representatives, Nepal Rastra Bank, and the finance ministry.

“We must review the rules and create an environment that makes it easier to build a global unicorn from Nepal,” Shah wrote. “IT products and exports are already in a promising position. We will ease taxes and reform policies, including the rules governing international earnings, so that talented young people and companies can earn more easily and reinvest their money.”

But industry leaders say ambitious promises alone will not be enough. They want the government to address a combination of high taxes, restrictions on cross-border payments, limited access to international digital payment platforms, and inadequate investment.

Developers say the tax burden on payments for overseas servers, advertising, and campaigns to attract international users can exceed 30 percent, and this significantly raises operating costs and leaves companies with less money to reinvest in product development and expansion.

Sujan Shakya, chief of Teslatech, the company behind globally popular game Callbreak, which has recorded more than 150 million downloads, says the high cost of international payments is undermining the competitiveness of Nepali developers.

“When we pay for overseas servers, advertising, and user acquisition, and on top of these we have to pay additional taxes of nearly 30 percent,” Shakya said. “That makes it extremely difficult to compete with foreign companies.”

The tax burden comprises 13 percent value-added tax, 15 percent tax deducted at source and 2 percent digital services tax.

Shakya wants the government to ease taxes on payments for international servers, advertising and user acquisition, which are essential for reaching and retaining users in overseas markets.

Another major obstacle is the inability of Nepali companies to open merchant accounts on the Google Play Store, developers say.

The restriction prevents local companies from selling in-app purchases, through which users pay for additional services, virtual items and other digital content while using a game or mobile application.

Without access to Google Play merchant accounts, Nepali developers are largely restricted to earning revenue through advertising, rather than tapping into the potentially more lucrative market for paid digital content.

Developers want the government to engage with Google and introduce the necessary policy changes to allow Nepali companies to access the merchant service.

Asim Basnet of Dark Matter Game Productions, which has developed games including Sprite Ninja, Ninja Hattori, and the children's game Kidsage, says the industry will struggle to scale up without a more supportive policy environment.

“Companies need to reinvest their foreign earnings to grow,” Basnet said. “But nearly 30 percent is lost to VAT and tax deducted at source. The government should ease the tax burden on an industry that earns foreign currency and allow companies greater freedom to reinvest their earnings.”

For developers, the problem goes beyond taxation. They say Nepal's policies do not adequately distinguish between companies providing outsourced software services and those developing and owning their own intellectual property.

NJ Subedi, founder of Yarsa Labs, whose Ludo game has surpassed 200 million downloads worldwide, says the distinction is important when designing policies to support the country's technology industry.

“Outsourcing businesses have limited scope to scale because they do not own the intellectual property they work on. They also bring little long-term value to Nepal and potentially accelerate brain drain,” Subedi said. “Companies that develop their own products retain intellectual property in Nepal, have greater growth potential and create opportunities for local talent at home.”

Subedi welcomed the prime minister’s interest in the industry, saying Nepali developers are already competitive with their counterparts in developed countries in areas such as artificial intelligence and developer tools.

They have access to similar platforms and technical capabilities, he said, adding, “What they lack are the capital and policy conditions needed to turn their technical expertise into globally competitive businesses.”

“Nepal has few investors with the capital to back companies at that scale, and local venture capital alone cannot provide sufficient funding,” he said. “Foreign investors are also reluctant to invest in Nepal-registered companies because of the country's policy and business environment.”

Subedi believes Nepal needs more open and investor-friendly policies, similar to those in Singapore or Dubai, to attract the international capital required to build technology companies capable of competing globally.

The lack of access to foreign investment is particularly significant for game developers, whose businesses often require substantial upfront spending on product development, marketing, infrastructure, and user acquisition before generating significant returns.

Industry leaders argue that allowing companies to retain and reinvest more of their foreign earnings, simplifying international transactions and opening access to global digital payment platforms would give them a better chance of scaling up.

They also want the government to recognise locally developed products as a distinct economic opportunity rather than treating all IT companies under the same regulatory framework.

Prime Minister Shah's renewed interest in gaming and esports is not entirely new. As Kathmandu mayor, he had pledged to support the esports industry. The Kathmandu Metropolitan City allocated Rs10 million for competitions in its 2022-23 budget.

The programme, however, was never implemented after the proposed spending attracted widespread criticism and controversy on social media and in public debate.

His latest pledge has once again raised expectations among developers. But they say the real test will be whether the government can translate its ambition of creating a global technology unicorn into concrete changes in taxation, foreign exchange rules, digital payment access and investment policy.

title: Three in four transport jobs in Nepal are informal - The Kathmandu Post
description: Three in four transport jobs in Nepal are informal  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nearly 73 percent of jobs in Nepal’s transport sector remain informal. Drivers, conductors, helpers, and other transport workers often lack written job contracts and have little or no social safety net, according to a new policy brief by the International Labour Organization (ILO).

The brief, ‘Informality in Nepal’s Transport Sector: Promoting enterprise formalisation and extending social protection to transport workers’, points to a critical gap between business registration and workers’ rights.

Although 89.5 per cent of transport establishments were registered in 2018, informal employment relationships remained widespread, with approximately 62 percent of jobs within formal enterprises still informal in 2022-23, the report said, highlighting how business registration has not necessarily led to employment formalisation.

The numbers are stark. Of 160 transport workers surveyed, none had a written employment contract, only three were enrolled in the Social Security Fund (SSF). Around 41 percent of informal employees earned below the minimum support wage, and informal transport workers were four times as likely to live in poverty as their formally employed counterparts.

Nepal’s transport sector supports economic activity and diverse forms of employment, yet many workers remain in informal jobs with limited access to decent working conditions and social protection. Transport contributes 6.73 percent of Nepal’s gross domestic product (GDP) and connects people, businesses and markets. Yet the drivers, conductors, and helpers who keep it running face unstable incomes, long hours, unsafe working conditions and little or no social protection, the brief says.

Numan Özcan, ILO Country Director for Nepal said, “A registered business is no guarantee of a protected worker. When nearly three in four transport jobs are informal, a licence on the wall changes nothing for the person behind the wheel. Workers need a written contract, a fair wage and social security that actually reaches them. Formalisation has to be measured in workers’ lives, not in registration certificates.”

The gap is following workers onto the apps. The brief notes that ride-hailing and delivery services are creating new income opportunities, but workers often lack written agreements, clear employment protections, and pathways into social security.

The ILO brief identifies eight priority actions to advance formalisation and extend social protection to transport workers. Key recommendations include making social security contributions more affordable and flexible for workers with irregular incomes, simplifying enterprise registration and compliance procedures, strengthening enforcement of minimum wages and labour standards, and establishing a clear legal framework to protect digital platform workers.

It also calls for better worker registration, accessible grievance mechanisms, and stronger measures to address occupational safety and gender-related risks.

The brief is blunt: formalisation cannot stop at registering businesses. It has to show up in workers’ lives, as fair wages, safer working conditions, employment security, and effective social protection.

By identifying practical pathways for reform, the brief offers policymakers, employer organisations, workers' organisations, and other stakeholders guidance on advancing inclusive and decent work conditions in Nepal’s transport sector. The recommendations can help inform Nepal’s ongoing efforts to strengthen its labour laws and policy frameworks and expand social protection coverage.

title: Nepal launches TikTok campaign to promote tourism to global audiences - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal launches TikTok campaign to promote tourism to global audiences  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal has formally launched a digital campaign in collaboration with social media platform TikTok to promote the country's tourism potential to global audiences.

The campaign, launched by the Nepal Tourism Board in partnership with the video platform, aims to showcase Nepal’s natural beauty, rich cultural heritage, historical sites and diverse tourism experiences for a vast range of viewers.

Running until the end of 2026, the initiative also seeks to connect local content creators, tourism businesses, entrepreneurs and communities with opportunities emerging from the digital economy.

Minister for Communications and Information Technology Bikram Timilsina, launching the collaboration on Friday, said digital platforms were playing an increasingly important role in how travellers discover destinations, make choices and plan their trips.

“Digital platforms have transformed ways the world discovers and becomes attracted to travel destinations. A story shared from one corner of the world can inspire someone in another corner to visit Nepal,” the minister said. “We welcome TikTok as a long-term partner in connecting Nepal’s tourism, culture, creativity and youth with the world.”

Sunil Sharma, acting director of the Public Relations and Promotion Department at the Nepal Tourism Board, described the partnership as an important step towards making the country's destination promotion strategy more effective.

“This campaign marks an important beginning in taking Nepal’s destination promotion efforts in a new direction,” Sharma said. “We expect to use the experience and lessons gained through our partnership with TikTok to expand cooperation with other international digital platforms and increase Nepal’s global reach and visibility.”

Emphasising that Nepal is not merely a destination to be seen but a country to be experienced, embraced and remembered for a lifetime, Sharma urged content creators to go beyond showcasing mountains and natural landscapes. He encouraged them to highlight the country's cultural diversity, natural heritage, local communities and distinctive tourism experiences.

Under the campaign, nine international travel content creators from Europe, the Middle East, Southeast Asia and South Asia are visiting various tourist destinations in Nepal and sharing their experiences with audiences worldwide. They are in Nepal from October 30 to November 7, 2026.

A dedicated hashtag page has also been launched on TikTok, allowing users to explore and share content related to Nepal. Similarly, through TikTok's collaboration feature, the campaign will bring together Nepali celebrities and local content creators to share authentic stories and experiences reflecting Nepal's identity with international audiences.

Live streaming from various tourist destinations across the country is another major component of the initiative.

Amir Galen, TikTok's head of government relations and public policy for the Middle East, Eurasia and Africa, said the partnership would bring Nepal's tourism potential to global audiences while creating opportunities for local creators and small businesses to benefit from the digital economy.

He said TikTok was keen to expand its collaboration with Nepal beyond tourism promotion to include community development, local entrepreneurship and greater international recognition of Nepali art and culture.

The campaign, which is aligned with the tourism promotion priorities of the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, is expected to strengthen cooperation among government agencies, the private sector, media organisations and digital content creators in promoting Nepal internationally.

title: Opinion | Can Nepal cook dal bhat on its own electricity? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Can Nepal cook dal bhat on its own electricity?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal has been talking about its energy future for years. We talk about hydropower, electricity exports, electric vehicles and reducing our dependence on imported petroleum products. But one part of that future deserves much more attention: the kitchen.

Every household cooks. Every hotel, restaurant, resort, café, canteen, tea shop and food business cooks. And much of that cooking still depends on imported cooking gas.

So this is a question of energy security, foreign currency and Nepal’s long-term future. As a chef who has worked in professional kitchens in Nepal and abroad, I have seen first-hand how important energy is to hospitality. Nepal should start planning now for a 10-year National Electric Cooking Mission: practical, affordable and gradual, and ready before the next cooking gas crisis.

Nepal does not produce the widely used Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) cooking gas; all of it comes from India. Official Foreign Trade Statistics show 514.34 million kilograms imported in fiscal year 2022/23, about 1,409 tonnes every day. The Department of Customs valued LPG imports at Rs62.58 billion in FY 2024/25, and at Rs52.21 billion in the first 11 months of FY 2025/26. Monthly demand sits at 45,000 to 50,000 tonnes , about a third of it from commercial users such as hotels and restaurants. These are tens of billions of rupees leaving Nepal every year to buy cooking fuel. And LPG is not a luxury. People need it every day.

The system is also fragile. In March, amid West Asia tensions, Nepal Oil Corporation began selling half-filled cylinders and queues formed at depots, even though imports had not fallen . That is exactly the lesson: A country does not have to run out of fuel to experience an energy crisis. The half-fill rule lasted months; restaurants and hotels said it was not enough for heavy-duty cooking , and shortages returned after full cylinders resumed. So why wait for the next crisis to prepare seriously for an alternative?

Nepal has another energy resource: electricity, produced at home. And Nepal does not need to start from zero. The government’s Energy Consumption Growth and Export Strategy, 2083 BS, proposes phasing out LPG subsidies by FY 2092/93, supporting electric stoves and raising per capita consumption to 1,500 kilowatt-hours by 2035. Consumers are already ahead of policy, with induction and infrared cooker imports surging . So instead of importing more fuel to cook food, can we increasingly use electricity produced in Nepal?

Let me be clear. I am not suggesting that every household throw away its gas stove tomorrow, or that LPG disappear overnight. Reliability, affordability, infrastructure and the different needs of urban and rural kitchens are real challenges, so the transition must be practical and gradual. The objective is to build an entire ecosystem around electric cooking, from households to hotels, hospitals and culinary schools.

First, the alternatives to LPG need to be made affordable. An induction cooker’s upfront cost of Rs5,000 to Rs6,000 is too high for many households. Nepal should examine reducing duties on induction cookers, electric pressure cookers, ovens and commercial induction systems, with targeted subsidies for lower-income households, gradually shifting support from imported fuel to domestic electricity.

Second, commercial kitchens need to be brought in. The debate focuses too much on households, yet hotels pay around Rs15 a unit for electricity, which discourages switching. Low-interest financing, equipment grants, help with electrical upgrades and a preferential tariff for verified electric cooking would change the maths. A restaurant should not carry the cost of a modern electric kitchen alone.

We also need to prove it with Nepali food. People don’t change technology because the government tells them to; they change when they see it work. Chefs, culinary schools, hotels and digital creators should show dal, bhat, tarkari, roti, momo, Newari, Thakali and Mithila food cooked electrically, and major hotels could each set up a demonstration electric kitchen for training, equipment testing and public awareness.

Also important is the need to fix the wires first. Electric cooking needs reliable electricity, and it is not enough to tell a family or a restaurant to buy an induction cooker if transformers, wiring and peak-hour capacity cannot cope. The government’s own strategy flags weak distribution. The Nepal Electricity Authority’s then chief estimated in 2022 that replacing every LPG cylinder in the Kathmandu Valley would need another 500 to 600 megawatts. Cooking policy and grid policy must move together.

We also need to collect real data and build an industry. A national programme bringing together government, the NEA, chefs, hotels, appliance makers, culinary schools and banks could set standards, financing models and training, and measure what a restaurant spends on LPG today and what the same kitchen would use in electricity. We should make the transition based on evidence, not slogans. It could also create jobs in installation, repair and kitchen design.

A roadmap could run in three stages, subject to proper technical and economic studies: 2027–2030, build the foundation; 2030–2033, accelerate adoption in households, hotels and institutions; 2033–2037, make electric cooking the preferred option for new homes and hospitality projects where technically appropriate. Each stage needs measurable targets: kitchens converted, LPG cut, foreign currency saved.

The debate should not be gas versus electricity. It should be imported energy versus energy we can increasingly produce ourselves. Electricity is not automatically cheaper in every kitchen; that depends on equipment, tariffs, infrastructure and cooking practice, which is why Nepal needs pilots and transparent data. But the strategic opportunity is too important to ignore.

I am not writing this as an energy economist. I am writing this as a chef. Every day, millions of Nepalis enter kitchens and turn energy into food, so our kitchens are part of Nepal’s energy future. Modern electric cooking does not mean giving up our food culture. Our food culture can remain traditional while our energy technology evolves.

We don’t have to wait for the next crisis. Planning during a crisis is expensive. Planning before a crisis is smart. Nepal can start building an alternative while LPG is still available. The question to ask is, “How can we use the electricity we generate in Nepal to cook the food we eat in Nepal?” Nepal needs a national plan for the kitchen of the future. And that future could increasingly be electric.

description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Nepal’s latest economic developments present a mixed picture of improving financial activity, expanding domestic economic initiatives and persistent structural vulnerabilities. Foreign grant receipts rose to Rs 7.985 billion in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026/27, reaching 12.93 percent of the annual target and significantly outperforming the corresponding period last year. Similarly, Prabhu Mahalaxmi Life Insurance reported a 45.88 percent increase in quarterly net profit, while manufacturing industries in Sudurpashchim operated at 51.29 percent of installed capacity, reflecting pockets of industrial growth.

However, the devastating August 26 Bhote Koshi floods have exposed substantial economic and infrastructure vulnerabilities. Damage to the energy sector alone reached Rs 132.83 billion, with recovery requirements estimated at Rs 218.58 billion. The financial sector faces an additional Rs 65.215 billion in rehabilitation costs, highlighting the wider economic consequences of natural disasters.

Meanwhile, government initiatives to strengthen social security for public procurement workers and promote indigenous products signal efforts to improve labour protection and stimulate domestic entrepreneurship. Tourism also showed encouraging momentum, with Mustang attracting 35,858 visitors during the festive period.

Overall, the developments suggest an economy with emerging growth opportunities but significant recovery, infrastructure resilience and employment challenges. Sustaining progress will require effective resource mobilisation, stronger disaster preparedness, industrial investment and broader participation in economic growth.

Gold remains at Rs 283,000 per tola, silver at Rs 3,810

Gold and silver prices remained unchanged in the domestic market on Sunday, maintaining the rates recorded on Friday. According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Associations, hallmark gold was traded at Rs 283,000 per tola (11.66 grams), while the price stood at Rs 242,625 per 10 grams. Similarly, silver was priced at Rs 3,810 per tola and Rs 3,266 per 10 grams. Both precious metals maintained their previous trading prices, according to the federation.

Foreign grant receipts reach Rs 7.985 billion in first quarter

Foreign grant inflows into the government treasury totalled Rs 7.985 billion during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026/27, showing a significant improvement over the same period last year. Data released by the Financial Comptroller General Office (FCGO) show that the amount received by mid-October accounted for 12.93 percent of the annual grant target of Rs 61.74 billion. During the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, the government had received approximately Rs 2 billion in foreign grants, equivalent to 3.76 percent of that year’s annual target. The latest figures indicate an improvement in the mobilisation of external grant resources during the opening months of the current fiscal year.

NPC estimates Rs 65.215 billion for financial sector recovery

The National Planning Commission has estimated that Rs 65.215 billion will be required to restore the financial sector following the devastating floods in Rasuwa on August 26. According to preliminary assessment findings, the disaster damaged 16 bank branches belonging to 12 commercial banks, affecting 78,204 depositors. It also disrupted non-hydropower-related loan investments worth Rs 2.43 billion. The combined financial losses suffered by the public and private sectors have been estimated at Rs 65.031 billion. The projected recovery requirement exceeds the initial losses, reflecting the additional costs associated with rebuilding damaged infrastructure and restoring services.

Bhote Koshi floods cause Rs 132.83 billion in energy sector losses

Preliminary findings of the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA), released by the National Planning Commission (NPC), have put the damage to Nepal’s energy sector from the August 26 Bhote Koshi floods at Rs 132.83 billion. The assessment estimates direct damage to physical assets at Rs 89.26 billion, while economic losses resulting from disrupted operations amount to Rs 43.56 billion. The floods affected 14 hydropower facilities, six substations and transmission networks in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts. The estimated cost of rehabilitating and rebuilding the affected energy infrastructure stands at Rs 218.58 billion, as authorities consider necessary changes to reconstruction and infrastructure design.

Government introduces minimum wage and social security provisions for public procurement workers

The government has introduced new guidelines to guarantee minimum wages, social security coverage and basic labour rights for workers hired through public procurement contracts, including those in construction, industrial, consultancy and information technology services. Under the new provisions, employers must register eligible workers with the Social Security Fund (SSF). For workers in construction and consultancy services, the government and employers are each required to contribute 10 percent towards the prescribed social security contribution. The guidelines also require employers to deposit workers’ wages directly into their bank accounts. Recruitment fees cannot be charged to workers, nor can employers recover payments through coercion or undue pressure. Other provisions include mandatory workplace safety arrangements, free worker registration and mechanisms for addressing labour-related complaints. Employers are required to resolve grievances within seven days, while repeated violations of labour regulations may result in blacklisting. Businesses that fail to enrol their workers in the Social Security Fund will also be disqualified from participating in public procurement processes.

NEA prepares festive power supply as peak demand projected at 1,700 MW

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has finalised operational arrangements to ensure an uninterrupted electricity supply throughout the Tihar and Chhath festivals. On Sunday, the authority issued directives to regional distribution centres, grid operation units and load dispatch teams to maintain round-the-clock technical standby services and complete pending transmission line maintenance works promptly. The NEA has projected that domestic electricity demand could reach 1,700 megawatts during the evening peak on Laxmi Puja. Against this, the country’s total domestic generation capacity is estimated at 2,500 MW, indicating sufficient capacity to meet anticipated consumption during the festive period. The authority expects the available generation capacity to ensure a reliable domestic supply without the need for electricity imports or load-shedding measures.

Government launches three-day Tihar fair to promote indigenous products

The government has launched a three-day Tihar Indigenous Products Fair in Kathmandu to promote locally produced goods and provide market opportunities for domestic entrepreneurs. The fair began on Sunday at the Bagmati provincial office premises of the Food Management and Trading Company in Thapathali. It features a range of locally produced goods, including indigenous agricultural products, traditional food items, flower garlands, earthenware, handicrafts and traditional cultural attire. Farmers, young entrepreneurs and women-led businesses are among the participants. The initiative aims to encourage consumers to purchase domestic products while connecting local producers with wider markets. The government also plans to replicate the fair’s model across all 77 districts, using public holidays and festive occasions to promote local production, entrepreneurship and small-scale businesses throughout the country.

Prabhu Mahalaxmi Life Insurance reports 45.88 percent rise in quarterly profit

Prabhu Mahalaxmi Life Insurance Company Limited recorded an unaudited net profit of Rs 93 million in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026/27, representing a 45.88 percent increase from Rs 63.7 million in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year. The company’s financial performance also improved in terms of premium collection, with gross premium income rising 30.25 percent to Rs 1.88 billion. Its life insurance fund expanded by 32.81 percent to reach Rs 19.718 billion during the review period. Based on its paid-up capital of Rs 5.307 billion, the company’s annualised earnings per share (EPS) stood at Rs 7.01. The quarterly results indicate growth in the company’s profitability, premium income and life insurance fund compared with the same period of fiscal year 2025/26.

Tourist arrivals in Mustang surpass 35,000 during festive season

Mustang welcomed more than 35,000 visitors during the Tihar holiday period, with favourable weather conditions contributing to increased tourist movement in the Himalayan district. According to the District Police Office, Mustang, a total of 35,858 tourists visited the district between October 18 and November 1. Of the total arrivals, 27,107 were domestic tourists and 8,751 were foreign visitors. The foreign tourist arrivals included 7,714 visitors from SAARC member countries and 1,037 from other nations. Many visitors travelled to Mustang for pilgrimage at the Muktinath Temple, while others explored the northern border area around Korala Pass and cultural heritage sites in settlements across the mountainous district. The favourable weather during the holiday period helped facilitate travel along high-altitude routes, contributing to the increase in visitor numbers.

Sudurpashchim industries operate at 51.29 percent of installed capacity

Manufacturing industries in Sudurpashchim Province operated at an average of 51.29 percent of their installed capacity, according to an annual economic activity report published by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB). The report, which covers 14 major manufacturing sectors, recorded substantial growth in several industrial activities. Wheat flour production increased by 137.17 percent, sugar processing by 134.67 percent and brick manufacturing by 100 percent. The province has registered 1,599 industrial units with a combined capital investment of Rs 2.223 billion. These industries provide direct employment to 5,452 people. The findings point to the contribution of manufacturing activities to employment generation, regional industrial development and the expansion of local economic opportunities.

title: The two Nepali border villages that empty for six months every year - The Kathmandu Post
description: The two Nepali border villages that empty for six months every year  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
As Tihar, Nepal’s second-biggest festival, begins, families nationwide are preparing to reunite, exchange colourful tika, and celebrate with marigold and globe amaranth (makhamali) garlands. Even those who could not return to their villages for Dashain are making plans to go home.

But for Anjani Bohara of Chhangru, a village on Nepal’s northwestern edge, this is the time to leave home.

Before her family moves out, it must store its harvest and prepare for six months away from home. “There’s so much to do before we leave. We have to get everything in order, both at home and on the farm,” she said.

Her 13-member family is busy gathering firewood, cutting and drying fodder for livestock, and collecting dried leaves to use as bedding when they return next April.

For six months of an unusually long winter, Tinkar and Chhangru endure heavy snowfall and extreme cold. Snow remains on the ground for long periods, making it difficult to live in either village. To escape the harsh conditions, residents will leave in the coming weeks and move temporarily to Khalanga, the district headquarters of Darchula, and other lower-lying areas.

Because they will not return until April, families are rushing to get everything in order. The seasonal migration, known locally as kuncha sarne , is repeated every year, but leaving home still requires extensive preparation. Residents must store enough food, arrange for their livestock and prepare their fields so that farming can resume as soon as they return. Their homes will remain locked and the villages deserted throughout the winter.

With no one left in the villages during the cold months, residents are working around the clock to finish their tasks. In Chhangru and Tinkar, which lie along Nepal’s borders with China and India, few people can be found idle. Some are threshing buckwheat harvested in April and May. Others are tying napal , a Tibetan variety of wheat, into small bundles with their stalks intact before storing it. Some are setting aside potatoes, beans, flour, and other food for the winter, while others are making dried preserves from choto , a large variety of radish.

Every household must complete its farm work before leaving. “Most people have already brought in their crops. Now we will start carrying manure from the cattle sheds to the fields,” said Bhupendra Tinkari of Tinkar. “Once that is done, we will sow coriander and mustard greens. By the time we return, they will have sprouted and be ready to eat in April.”

Residents also sow garlic and peas before leaving. The seeds germinate in their absence and are ready for tending when families return. Manure piled in the fields now is spread over the soil after their return, before the next round of cultivation begins, Tinkari said.

Tinkar has 75 households and Chhangru 124, with a combined population of around 1,200. Both villages fall under ward 1 of Byas Rural Municipality in Darchula district. In about two weeks, towards mid-November, both will be completely deserted for the next six months.

“The village is completely deserted in winter. Everyone moves down to the lowlands,” Tinkari said.

The seasonal migration, known in the local language as kuncha sarne , has been practised for generations by the Sauka community, which inhabits the two villages. Before leaving, families must secure enough food to last the year and prepare their farmland for the next planting season. They spend six months in their high-altitude villages during the farming season and the remaining six months in the lowlands to escape the winter.

“We may leave because of the cold, but we have to come back in the monsoon. That is why we must make arrangements not just for now but also for when we return,” said Hitesh Budhathoki, a ward member of Byas Rural Municipality-1. “Getting everything ready before leaving makes things easier when we come back.”

Chhangru and Tinkar, both in the high Himalayas, have only one farming season a year. Livestock rearing is the main source of income for residents, and the animals also move with their owners during the seasonal migration. Once the farm work is complete, families pack food, bedding and household essentials and set out with their animals.

The journey to the lowlands takes about a week on foot, through Indian territory.

“We take the milking cows with us wherever we go,” said Droupati Aitwal of Chhangru. “We leave the other animals at places along the route where there is good grazing, under the care of herders. We bring them back with us when we return.”

Families hire herders collectively and share the cost according to the number of animals each household leaves behind, she said.

The journey is particularly difficult for children, new mothers, pregnant women, elderly people, people with disabilities and women travelling with livestock.

“It is difficult, but we have no option. This has been the practice since our great-grandparents’ time. We cannot stay in the villages because the snow and cold make it impossible,” Aitwal said.

Before the migration, each household performs rituals to worship its family deity. Families invite the wider community and host feasts. A collective worship ceremony is held at the end, and residents leave the villages on the same day.

“Before leaving home for the winter, we pray for the safety, well-being and prosperity of our families and community. Only after the worship is completed do we consider the preparations for departure formally finished,” said 80-year-old Devalal Budhathoki of Tinkar.

As the date approaches, families finish storing their harvest, preparing their fields, arranging care for their animals and performing the rituals. They then set off in a long procession.

Once residents of Chhangru and Tinkar descend on the district headquarters and other low-lying areas, life along this remote stretch of the border comes to a standstill. Doors are locked, daily activities cease, and the villages remain silent until spring.

When families return around April, they unlock their houses and resume their routines. Garlic, mustard greens, coriander and peas sown before their departure are sprouted in the fields and are ready for care. Farming, livestock rearing and village life gradually return to their usual rhythm. When winter comes again, the preparations to leave begin anew.

The cycle has continued in Chhangru and Tinkar for centuries.

A perennial struggle with the trail

As residents prepare to move to the lowlands for winter, they face another familiar worry: the route out of their villages.

Travelling through Nepal is far from easy. Landslides have damaged several stretches of the trail connecting Tinkar and Chhangru, while the mule track from Chhangru to Dumling is also in poor condition.

Residents say movement for both people and livestock is difficult because sections of the trail around Budi Khola, Mausyabhir, Ghatibagar, Dopkhe, Tambaku and Kaljul have been damaged.

“Everyone in the villages is preparing to move, but there is no reliable route through our own country,” said resident Dan Singh Tinkari. “We have to suffer every year because the trail is in such poor condition.”

Some sections of the route between Tinkar and Chhangru have been patched up with help from residents, the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police, but the trail remains far from fully repaired, he said.

The federal, provincial and local governments have spent money on repairing and rebuilding the mule track, but the problems persist. Four years ago, around Rs15.4 million was spent on the route, including Rs10.8 million through the Nepal Army, Rs3 million from the Sudurpaschim provincial government and Rs1.6 million from Byas Rural Municipality.

Yet the route remains difficult to use, forcing residents to continue travelling through India.

In previous years, residents were even held up in Khalanga when they tried to move their villages for the winter because of poor roads and problems at the border crossing. They staged a sit-in outside the District Administration Office, bringing their livestock with them.

For the Byansi community, the absence of a safe and reliable mule track has made the twice-yearly seasonal migration increasingly challenging.

The distance involved makes it difficult for the rural municipality to build a durable route using its own budget, said Dharam Raj Joshi, chief administrative officer of Byas Rural Municipality.

KATHMANDU: Weather conditions are expected to remain mostly fair across the country on Monday, although some mountainous and hilly areas may experience partial cloud cover, with chances of light rain and snowfall in a few locations.

According to the Weather Forecasting Division, partly cloudy conditions are likely in the mountainous and hilly regions of Gandaki, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces, as well as in the mountainous areas of Koshi, Bagmati and Lumbini provinces during the daytime.

The Division has forecast the possibility of light rain or snowfall at a few places in the mountainous and hilly regions of Gandaki, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces, along with the mountainous regions of Koshi and Bagmati provinces.

During the night, partly cloudy conditions are expected to persist in the mountainous regions, while most other parts of the country are likely to experience generally fair weather. A few places in the mountainous regions of Gandaki and Karnali provinces may receive light rain or snowfall.

Despite the generally favourable weather outlook, people travelling to high-altitude destinations and mountain regions are advised to remain mindful of possible changes in weather conditions, particularly where light snowfall is forecast.
